task_title: Intercepting and Tracking Navigational Systems and DME Arcs
objective: By the end of this lesson you can tune, identify and check a VOR or GPS, find your position, intercept and track a radial, course or DME arc solely by instruments within ACS limits, and recognize and report a navigation failure.
why: Every IFR route, arrival and approach starts with getting onto a course and staying there. When GPS quits or a NAVAID goes off the air, you must still know where you are and fly the course by hand.

prereading.what: VOR system, the VOR indicator, orientation, tracking to and from the station, course interception and VOR common errors.
prereading.label: IFH Ch 9, 9-8 to 9-16

prereading.what: VOR checks, DME, flying a DME arc, intercepting lead radials and slant range error.
prereading.label: IFH 9-17 to 9-19

prereading.what: How GPS works, RAIM, GPS substitution for DME (including DME arcs), GPS CDI sensitivity and GPS errors.
prereading.label: IFH 9-26 to 9-31

prereading.what: VOR identification and accuracy, the VOR MON, VOR receiver checks and DME.
prereading.label: AIM 1-1-3 to 1-1-7

prereading.what: GPS: RAIM, IFR equipment rules, database checks and CDI sensitivity.
prereading.label: AIM 1-1-17

prereading.what: Using GPS on conventional routes and procedures (including DME arcs) and handling GPS jamming or spoofing.
prereading.label: AIM 1-2-3 to 1-2-4

prereading.what: Automation management: anticipate, act, verify, and choosing the right level of automation.
prereading.label: RMH Ch 7, 7-1 to 7-3

warmup: You are in the clouds, the GPS just showed an integrity alert, and ATC asks you to join the 15 DME arc. What would you look at first to know where you are, and which radio would you trust?

key_terms.def: A magnetic course going out FROM a VOR station, like a spoke on a wheel.
The knob you turn to pick the course on a VOR indicator.
The needle or bar that shows if you are left or right of the selected course.
Shows if the selected course, flown as set, takes you TO or FROM the station. It does not show where the nose points.
A heading indicator and CDI in one instrument, giving a top-down picture of you and the course.
The needle shows the opposite of normal, so you must turn away from it to get back on course.
The space right over a VOR where the signal is weak and the needle swings.
DME distance measured in a straight line from the airplane to the station, not along the ground.
The radial where you start the turn from a DME arc onto the inbound course.
Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring: the GPS receiver checking that its own satellite signals can be trusted.
Wide Area Augmentation System: ground stations and satellites that make GPS more accurate and monitor its integrity.
How many miles a full-scale GPS CDI deflection means: ±5 NM en route, ±1 NM terminal, ±0.3 NM on final.

chunks.title: The VOR system and the radio

body.p: The VOR is oriented to magnetic north and sends 360 courses TO or FROM the station. A VOR with DME is a VOR/DME. A VOR with military TACAN is a VORTAC, which gives both direction and distance [[23:251|IFH 9-8]].

Courses going out FROM the station are called radials. Think of the spokes of a wheel: at any moment you are on one radial. VOR information does not change with your heading or attitude [[23:253|IFH 9-10]].

head: Item
What to know
rows: 108.0 to 117.95 MHz. From 108.0 to 112.0, VORs use even tenths; localizers use odd tenths [[23:254|IFH 9-11]]
Line of sight; range grows with your altitude [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3]]. Coverage is typically at least 40 miles at normal IFR altitudes [[23:253|IFH 9-10]]
Morse code, or a recorded voice saying the name followed by "VOR". This is the only positive way to identify it [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3]]

callout.text: No ident, or a T-E-S-T code, means the station is under maintenance and may be unreliable even if the needle looks good [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]]. Never fly a procedure that is NOTAMed out of service, even if the ident is present [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]].

body.p: If your radio decodes the identifier and shows it on screen, you do not have to listen to the audio ident [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]]. Otherwise, turn up the volume and listen before you rely on the needle [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].

The FAA is shutting down some VORs. It keeps a backup network (the VOR MON) so that anywhere in the contiguous U.S. you are within 100 NM of an airport with an approach that does not need GPS [[33:70|AIM 1-1-3]].

check.q: Your VOR shows a good needle but you hear no Morse ident. Can you use it?
check.a: No. A missing ident means the station may be off the air for maintenance and unreliable [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]].

bullets: OBS: turn it to set the course under the course index [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].
CDI: centers when you are on the selected radial or its reciprocal. Full deflection means 12° or more off course. The edge of the center circle is 2°, and each dot adds about 2° [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].
TO/FROM: shows if the selected course takes you TO or FROM the station. It does not show which way you are heading [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].
Flag: an OFF or NAV flag (or a blank TO/FROM window) means the signal is too weak to use [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].

body.p: **To find your radial:** tune, identify, then turn the OBS until the needle centers with a FROM showing. The index now shows the radial you are on. The course inbound to the station is its reciprocal [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

In this figure, the CDI is centered on 180°. With TO, you are north of the station on the 360° radial, and a course of 180° takes you to it. With FROM, you are on the 180° radial. The heading does not matter [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
One VOR puts you on a line. To fix your exact spot on that line you need a second NAVAID, such as another VOR radial or DME [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

callout.text: FROM + centered = "I am ON this radial." TO + centered = "This course takes me TO the station." The nose does not matter.

check.q: You center the CDI and read 090° FROM. Where are you, and what course flies you to the station?
check.a: East of the station on the 090° radial. Fly 270° inbound, the reciprocal [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

chunks.title: CDI or HSI, and reverse sensing

body.p: An HSI combines the heading indicator and the CDI. The picture shows where you are and which way you point, which lowers workload for intercepts, back courses and holding entries [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].

head: Standard VOR CDI
HSI
rows: No. The VOR shows the same thing no matter where the nose points [[23:254|IFH 9-11]]
Yes. Compass card is under the course arrow, like looking down on your airplane [[23:118|IFH 5-23]]
TO or FR in a window [[23:254|IFH 9-11]]
Triangle pointing to the head of the arrow = TO; to the tail = FROM [[23:118|IFH 5-23]]
Happens if the OBS is set to the reciprocal of your course. Then turn away from the needle [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]
Eliminated if the course arrow is set to the course you are flying (front course on a back course) [[29:216|IPH 4-76]]
Usually driven by a flux gate. If not, check it against the magnetic compass and reset it [[23:118|IFH 5-23]]

callout.text: Avoid reverse sensing the easy way: always set the OBS or course arrow to the course you intend to fly [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

body.p: On a glass panel, the HSI on the PFD works the same way. It shows the course pointer, CDI, heading bug and selected course [[23:255|IFH 9-12]].

check.q: You fly heading 180° outbound on the 180° radial but set 360° on a standard CDI. The needle goes right. Which way do you turn?
check.a: Left, away from the needle. The OBS is set to the reciprocal, so you have reverse sensing [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

body.p: First find where you are relative to the station and the course. Then pick an intercept heading. IFH steps (you may skip steps 1 to 3 if you turn straight to an intercept heading) [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]:

bullets: 1. Find the difference between the radial to intercept and the radial you are on. IFH example: 205° - 160° = 45° [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
2. Double it for the intercept angle, but never less than 20° or more than 90°. Example: 45° × 2 = 90° [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
3. Set the OBS to the desired radial or inbound course [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
4. Turn to the intercept heading [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
5. Hold it until the CDI centers. With practice, lead the turn so you do not overshoot [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
6. Turn to the magnetic heading of the course and track it [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

body.p: In Figure 9-16 you are inbound on the 160° radial and want the 205° radial inbound, a course of 025°. The intercept angle is 90°, so you fly heading 295°, which points 90° toward the course. As the needle centers, lead the turn to 025° [[23:258|IFH 9-15]].

callout.text: Intercept heading = the course you want, turned toward the course by the intercept angle. Picture it first: "Is the course to my left or right?"

body.p: To intercept a radial outbound, center the CDI with FROM to see where you are, set the radial under the index, and hold the intercept heading until the CDI centers. Or fly over the station and turn outbound [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

callout.text: First parallel the course (turn to its heading) if you are confused. Pilots think left and right of course, so lining up with the course makes the picture clear [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

check.q: You are on the 070° radial and want the 100° radial. What intercept angle does the IFH method give?
check.a: 60°: the difference is 30°, doubled is 60°, which is between 20° and 90° [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

chunks.title: Tracking with wind, and station passage

body.p: **To track TO the station:** set the course with TO showing and center the CDI. Fly the course under the index. If the needle moves left, the wind is from the left. Follow the needle with a 20° correction to the left [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

**Bracketing:** when the 20° correction brings the needle back to center, cut the correction in half. Now the needle should move much more slowly, and smaller corrections will do. Keep narrowing until you find the heading that holds the needle centered [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

head: Step
Heading (course 360°, wind from the left)
Why
rows: Start with a 20° correction toward the needle [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]

body.p: Do not change the OBS while tracking. Re-centering the needle and flying the new number is homing, which flies a curved path to the station [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

**Station passage.** A steady needle drift means you are drifting off course. A rapid or swinging needle means station passage is near. Over the station you fly through the zone of confusion [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. Use the TO/FROM change to confirm positive station passage, because some stations show brief needle swings that look like station passage [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]].

callout.text: On a radio without an OFF flag, transmitting on the combined NAV/COM can make the TO/FROM flicker like station passage. Read TO/FROM, CDI and OBS together, and never use a VOR reading taken while you transmit [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

body.p: Tracking outbound works the same: set the radial with FROM and correct toward the needle [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. ACS limit: no more than ¾-scale CDI deflection (ACS IR.V.A.S6). On a VOR, full scale is about 10° to 12° each side of center [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

check.q: Tracking inbound, your 20° left correction has just centered the needle. What next?
check.a: Cut the correction in half (10° left of course) and watch the needle; make smaller corrections from there [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

chunks.title: Checking the VOR: tests and rules

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.171: to fly IFR using VORs, the VOR equipment must be maintained under an approved procedure, or checked within the preceding 30 days and found within limits [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]].

head: Check
Maximum error
rows: VOT (FAA test signal) or repair-station test signal at the departure airport
Designated checkpoint on the departure airport surface
Designated airborne checkpoint (if no test signal or surface checkpoint)
No signal or point: airway radial over a prominent ground point, preferably more than 20 NM from the VOR, at a reasonably low altitude
Dual VORs (independent except the antenna) tuned to the same station

body.p: Log it: date, place, bearing error, and your signature in the aircraft log or other record [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

**Using a VOT:** tune the VOT frequency and center the CDI. The OBS should read 0° with FROM, or 180° with TO. An RMI reads 180° on any OBS setting [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]]. VOT, checkpoint locations and airborne checkpoints are in the Chart Supplement [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]].

callout.text: VOT: "Cessna 182" = Center the needle, 180 TO (or 0 FROM).

body.p: **Sensitivity check:** turn the OBS until the needle moves from center to the last dot. It should take no more than 10° to 12° each side [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]. Some propeller rpm settings can make the CDI swing up to ±6°; change rpm slightly before you blame the station or radio [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]].
Also required for IFR: two-way radio and navigation equipment suitable for the route [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(2)]].

check.q: At a VOT the CDI centers with the OBS on 183° and TO showing. Pass or fail?
check.a: Pass. It should read 180° TO, and 3° is within the ±4° limit for a test signal [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]] [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]].

body.p: The airplane's DME sends pulses, the ground station replies, and the radio turns the round-trip time into nautical miles [[33:72|AIM 1-1-7]]. With a VOR, DME gives you an exact position: bearing plus distance [[23:260|IFH 9-17]].

bullets: Accuracy: better than ½ mile or 3% of the distance, whichever is greater. Reliable up to 199 NM at line-of-sight altitude [[33:72|AIM 1-1-7]].
The DME ident is a higher tone, heard about once for every three or four VOR idents. If you hear only one ident about every 30 seconds, the DME works but the VOR may not [[23:260|IFH 9-17]].
Groundspeed shown by DME is accurate only when you fly directly to or from the station [[23:260|IFH 9-17]].
Many DMEs are tuned with a VHF NAV radio; a HOLD function keeps the DME on the last station [[23:260|IFH 9-17]].

body.p: **Slant range.** DME measures the straight line from your antenna to the station, not ground distance. The error is biggest close to the station; right over it, the DME shows your height above it in NM. The error is negligible if you are 1 mile or more from the station for each 1,000 ft above it [[23:262|IFH 9-19]].

callout.text: GPS distance is horizontal, so it can read a bit less than DME when you are high and close [[23:262|IFH 9-19]]. A DME/DME fix is more accurate than a VOR/DME fix [[23:262|IFH 9-19]].

check.q: You are 4,000 ft above a VORTAC. Beyond what distance can you ignore slant range error?
check.a: About 4 NM: 1 NM for each 1,000 ft above the facility [[23:262|IFH 9-19]].

chunks.title: Flying a DME arc and lead radials

body.p: A DME arc is part of the approach, not a feeder route. Once on it you have left the en route phase [[29:183|IPH 4-43]]. An arc must be based on a DME that has a VOR, because a LOC DME gives no all-around course information [[29:183|IPH 4-43]].
**Joining the arc (IFH example, 10 DME arc of OKT):** [[23:260|IFH 9-17]]

bullets: 1. Track inbound on the OKT 325° radial, checking DME often.
2. At 150 knots or less, a 0.5 NM lead works: start the turn at 10.5 DME. Faster, use a proportionately greater lead.
3. Turn about 90°. With no wind, roll out on 055°.
4. Watch the DME during the last part of the turn. Overshooting (more than 1.0 NM)? Keep turning past 055°. Undershooting? Roll out early.

body.p: Outbound to the same arc, the lead point is 10 - 0.5 = 9.5 NM [[23:261|IFH 9-18]].
**Holding the arc with an RMI or bearing pointer** [[23:261|IFH 9-18]]:

bullets: Put the pointer on the wingtip reference (90° or 270°) at the arc distance. Hold heading and let the pointer drift 5° to 10° behind the wingtip. Then turn toward the station to put it 5° to 10° ahead, and repeat. You fly a series of short straight legs.
Wind pushing you away from the station: keep the pointer ahead of the wingtip. Wind pushing you toward it: keep it behind.
Range corrections: change the relative bearing 10° to 20° for each ½ mile off the arc. Example: ½ to 1 mile outside with the pointer on the wingtip, turn 20° toward the station.

body.p: **Holding the arc with a CDI only:** after the 90° turn, center the CDI. Your heading is near the 90° or 270° side of the instrument. Each time the CDI gets 2° to 4° from center, re-center it and note the new heading [[23:261|IFH 9-18]]. Staying slightly inside the arc helps, because the arc then curves toward you [[23:261|IFH 9-18]].

**Lead radials.** A lead radial (LR) is where you start the turn from the arc to the inbound course. For most general aviation arcs at 150 knots or less, the lead is under 5° [[23:261|IFH 9-18]]. When the arc meets the course at more than 90°, the chart shows a lead radial giving at least 2 NM of lead [[29:183|IPH 4-43]]. Set the new course as soon as you can, and start the turn at the lead radial [[23:261|IFH 9-18]].

callout.text: Intercepting a localizer from an arc: at the lead radial, a single VOR/LOC receiver gets switched to the localizer. With two, keep one on the VOR and set the other to the LOC. In the IFH example the lead radial gives 7° of lead, so use a half-standard-rate turn until the LOC needle starts to move [[23:262|IFH 9-19]].

check.q: Inbound on a radial at 120 knots to join the 12 DME arc. When do you start the turn?
check.a: At about 12.5 DME. A 0.5 NM lead works at 150 knots or less [[23:260|IFH 9-17]].

chunks.title: GPS and WAAS: equipment, RAIM and the database

body.p: GPS needs at least four satellites above the mask angle for a 3-D position [[33:89|AIM 1-1-17]]. It figures distance and bearing to a waypoint from your position and its database [[23:269|IFH 9-26]].

head: Topic
The rule
rows: IFR GPS must meet TSO-C129(), C196(), C145() or C146(). VFR and hand-held units are not for IFR navigation [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17]] [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]
To detect a bad satellite: 5 satellites, or 4 plus baro-aiding. To also exclude it (FDE): 6, or 5 plus baro-aiding [[33:89|AIM 1-1-17]]
Two kinds: not enough satellites for RAIM, or RAIM found a possible error. Without RAIM you have no assurance of GPS accuracy [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]]
Needs another approved, working way to navigate the route, such as VOR. You must actively monitor it only when RAIM is lost [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]
Use other approved navigation, reroute, delay, or cancel [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]

TSO-C145()/C146(). WAAS monitors GPS and WAAS satellites and provides integrity [[33:103|AIM 1-1-18]]. Ground-based nav equipment is not required for en route IFR, but have a backup plan [[33:94|AIM 1-1-17]]

body.p: To keep baro-aiding working, enter the current altimeter setting into the receiver as the manual says [[33:89|AIM 1-1-17]].

**Database.** It must be current and right for the region [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]. Preflight: confirm the date of use is before expiration and look for provider notices. In flight: waypoint names must match the chart exactly, and the waypoints must be in a logical place and order [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]] [[33:93|AIM 1-1-17]]. Approaches must be loaded by name, never as hand-entered waypoints [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].
**NOTAMs.** Before any GPS IFR flight, review GPS and WAAS NOTAMs [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]. The government runs GPS tests that interfere with the signal; they are announced by NOTAM [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]].

callout.text: Know your box. Brands and even models work differently, so learn it with the manual, the AFM supplement and the built-in simulator before using it under IFR [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

check.q: Your non-WAAS IFR GPS predicts no RAIM at your ETA. Name your choices.
check.a: Rely on other approved navigation (like VOR), reroute to where RAIM is available, delay, or cancel [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

chunks.title: GPS course guidance, CDI scaling and arcs by GPS

body.p: A GPS CDI shows distance off course in miles, not degrees. How many miles full scale means depends on the phase of flight:

head: Phase
Full-scale CDI
rows: Terminal: within 30 NM of the airport with the approach armed, and on departures
Approach: ramps from 2 NM before the final approach waypoint

body.p: The ACS limit is ¾-scale deflection on whatever CDI scale is showing (ACS IR.V.A.S6). As the scale tightens from ±5 to ±1 to ±0.3 NM, the same needle position means fewer miles off course [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17]].

callout.text: As scaling tightens near the FAWP, a needle that is not centered moves out even on a good intercept heading. Get established before the ramp-down, and avoid vectors that join final within 2 NM of the FAWP [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17]].

body.p: **Picking a course to a waypoint.** For holding and for vectors to final, use the receiver's nonsequencing mode (often called OBS or HOLD) and set the course, much like a VOR [[23:271|IFH 9-28]] [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17]]. Know what bank angle your receiver uses for turn anticipation [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17]].

**GPS on conventional procedures.** A suitable IFR GPS can find your position from a VOR or DME fix, navigate to or from a VOR or NDB, hold over them, and fly a DME arc [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]]. It even works when the NAVAID is out of service or you have no DME [[33:116|AIM 1-2-3]]. You may need to tell ATC you are doing this [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]]. The database should stay current for the whole flight [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]].

bullets: IFH technique to fly a DME arc by GPS: check integrity is OK, make the DME facility the arc is based on the active waypoint, and hold the arc using GPS distance instead of DME. If that facility is not in the database, you may not do it [[23:270|IFH 9-27]].
Over a DME fix: you are there when GPS distance from the charted DME facility equals the charted DME and you are on the right course [[23:270|IFH 9-27]].
Waypoints must come from a current database, and the CDI must be on terminal (1 NM) sensitivity when tracking GPS course guidance in the terminal area [[23:270|IFH 9-27]].

Not allowed: flying a localizer course without raw LOC data, or replacing the NAVAID that gives lateral guidance on a final approach (unless the title says "or GPS") [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]] [[33:118|AIM 1-2-3]].

body.p: **Use the map.** A moving map shows you relative to NAVAIDs, waypoints, airspace and terrain [[23:29|IFH 1-10]]. Set map scale for en route or terminal work and choose north up, track up, DTK up or heading up [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]]. The PFD can show DTK (desired track) and TRK (actual track) [[23:255|IFH 9-12]]. The gap between heading and track is your wind drift [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]].

check.q: You must fly the 12 DME arc of a VORTAC but have no DME. What do you load as the active GPS waypoint?
check.a: The VORTAC the arc is based on. Fly the arc by GPS distance from it. If it is not in the database, you can't do it [[23:270|IFH 9-27]].

body.p: **Before the intercept:**

bullets: 1. VOR: tune, identify (audio or decoded ident), and check for flags [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3]] [[23:254|IFH 9-11]]. Confirm the 30-day VOR check is logged [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171]].
2. GPS: confirm integrity is good and the database is current; load waypoints from the database [[23:270|IFH 9-27]] [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].
3. Find your position: center the CDI with FROM, or read the GPS bearing and distance [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
4. Set the course you will fly (avoid reverse sensing) and picture where it is [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

body.p: **Intercept and track:**

bullets: 5. Pick an intercept angle (20° to 90°) and turn to the intercept heading [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
6. Hold heading, altitude and airspeed while you wait. Watch the needle's rate of movement and lead the turn [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
7. Roll out on course, then bracket: 20° correction, then half, then smaller [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
8. Check the map and the TRK readout to confirm your track matches the course [[23:29|IFH 1-10]] [[23:255|IFH 9-12]].

body.p: **With the autopilot (if the examiner asks):** set the course, use heading mode to fly the intercept heading, arm the nav mode, and watch the mode annunciators. White usually means armed; green means engaged [[30:52|RMH 7-3]]. Anticipate, act, verify [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

head: ACS standard
Tolerance
rows: No more than ¾-scale CDI deflection (ACS IR.V.A.S6)

callout.text: Trim first. A trimmed airplane holds altitude and airspeed while your eyes work the CDI, DME and map.

check.q: You are 1.2 NM outside a 10 DME arc. Are you within ACS limits, and what do you do?
check.a: No, the limit is ±1 NM (ACS IR.V.A.S6). Turn 20° or more toward the station to return to the arc [[23:261|IFH 9-18]].

chunks.title: Risk: automation, distraction, limits and failures

body.p: **Automation (R1).** Automation should cut workload, but it can confuse you, lead to errors or lull you into complacency [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]. A change in nav source can drop the autopilot to a lower mode, such as wings level [[30:52|RMH 7-3]]. One of the most common errors is not stepping down to a lower level of automation when things change [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]. If automation does not do what you expect, reduce the level, fly by hand and sort it out [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

**Distraction and lost awareness (R2).** Situational awareness means knowing your position, flight path, traffic, environment and human factors [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. With glass panels, stop, look and read before you push buttons [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]]. Following only the magenta line can lead you into trouble [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]]. Feeling rushed? Ask ATC for a delay or a vector [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

head: System limits (R3)
What can go wrong
rows: Line of sight [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3]]; roughness and needle swings near some stations; propeller rpm can cause ±6° swings [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]]
Slant range near the station; groundspeed only good direct to or from it [[23:262|IFH 9-19]] [[23:260|IFH 9-17]]
Antenna shadowed in a bank, valleys in high terrain, interference from portable radios [[23:274|IFH 9-31]]; jamming and spoofing [[33:118|AIM 1-2-4]]
AFMs prohibit using it as the primary data source [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]]

body.p: **Signs of GPS jamming or spoofing:** a big jump in GPS position, wrong clock time, position-error warnings, or other pilots reporting position errors [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]] [[33:120|AIM 1-2-4]]. Crosscheck with VOR or DME, be ready to fly conventional procedures, and tell ATC promptly [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]] [[33:120|AIM 1-2-4]]. Switch to another nav source and ask for an amended clearance if needed [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.187: under IFR in controlled airspace, report any in-flight nav, approach or com malfunction to ATC as soon as practical. Include aircraft ID, equipment affected, how much your IFR capability is hurt, and what help you want [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]. If your GPS fails, also amend your equipment suffix [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

body.p: **SRM (S10).** Use every resource: ATC and Flight Service are part of your team, and declaring an emergency gets you priority [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. With two pilots, one flies and one monitors, and both say what they intend [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

check.q: Your VOR receiver dies while you are on an IFR airway in the clouds. What four things go in your report to ATC?
check.a: Aircraft ID, the equipment affected, how much your IFR capability is impaired, and the help you want [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]].

body.p: The IFH lists these VOR errors [[23:257|IFH 9-14]] [[23:259|IFH 9-16]]:

bullets: Careless tuning and identification of the station.
Not checking the receiver for accuracy and sensitivity.
Turning the wrong way during orientation, common until you picture your position instead of the needle.
Not checking TO/FROM, especially on course reversals, which gives reverse sensing and wrong corrections.
Not paralleling the desired radial first on an intercept problem.
Overshooting and undershooting radials on intercepts.
Overcontrolling corrections while tracking, especially close to the station.
Misreading station passage (for example, needle flicker while transmitting).
Chasing the CDI, which turns tracking into homing. Careless heading control and not bracketing cause it.

body.p: GPS and automation errors to add: flying with an expired database or unchecked waypoints [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]], forgetting to arm the approach so the CDI stays at en route scale [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17]], and not verifying the autopilot mode after a change [[30:52|RMH 7-3]].

check.q: Why does chasing the CDI end up as homing?
check.a: You keep turning to center the needle instead of holding a corrected heading, so you fly a curved path. Bracket the wind correction instead [[23:259|IFH 9-16]] [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart: VOT table, checkpoint sign and DME fix symbols

body.p: A VOT list gives the airport and the test frequency. In the example, Groton is 110.25 and Hartford is 108.20 [[29:90|IPH Figure 2-50]]. On the test signal, set the course selector to 0 and the track bar should center with FROM showing. Set 180 and it should center with TO. The most error allowed is plus or minus 4 degrees [[29:90|IPH p 90]] [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]].

A checkpoint sign marks the spot on the airport where the signal is strong enough to check your VOR [[29:90|IPH p 90]]. The sign here reads VOR 116.4 and 147 degrees 4.1 NM. Tune 116.4 and the VOR should show the 147 degree radial. A DME should show 4.1 NM. The limit is again plus or minus 4 degrees [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(2)]].

On the en route chart, an arrow beside a fix shows which facility forms it. On a VHF chart it points away from that NAVAID. A DME fix has its own symbol, and the distance is the same as the airway mileage. When the mileage is not obvious, an encircled arrow gives it. In the example, 5 NM plus 10 NM gives 15 in the encircled arrow [[2:82|Chart Users' Guide p 82]].
Remember the paperwork too. The check must be within the last 30 days, and you record the date, place, bearing error and your signature [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)(2)]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

scenario.title: The arc, the jammed GPS and the busy cockpit
scenario.setup: You are single pilot, IFR in the clouds, in a single-engine airplane with a WAAS GPS navigator, one VOR/LOC receiver, no DME, and an autopilot with heading and nav modes. ATC clears you to join the 15 DME arc of a VORTAC to the approach. Your briefing showed a GPS test NOTAM near your route. Halfway around the arc, with the autopilot coupled to GPS, the map position jumps two miles and a GPS position-error message appears. A passenger starts asking questions.

questions.q: Was it legal to accept a DME arc with no DME on board?
questions.a: Yes, with a suitable IFR GPS. You may fly an arc based on DME using GPS [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]]: make the VORTAC the arc is based on the active waypoint and hold the arc by GPS distance, as long as it is in the current database [[23:270|IFH 9-27]].

questions.q: The position jumps and an error message appears. What do you suspect, and what do you do?
questions.a: Possible jamming or spoofing: a big position shift and position-error warnings are typical signs [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]] [[33:120|AIM 1-2-4]]. Crosscheck with the VOR, be ready to fly conventional procedures, and tell ATC promptly [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]] [[33:120|AIM 1-2-4]]. Change nav source and ask for an amended clearance [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]]. The NOTAM is no excuse to stay quiet here: in a NOTAMed test area you report when you need ATC help, and losing your arc guidance is that case [[33:120|AIM 1-2-4]].

questions.q: Without GPS or DME, can you keep flying the arc? What do you tell ATC?
questions.a: No. You have no distance source left for the arc, only a VOR radial. Report the malfunction: aircraft ID, equipment affected, how your IFR capability is impaired, and the help you want, such as vectors or a VOR-based approach [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]].

questions.q: You switch the CDI from GPS to VOR and the autopilot goes to wings level. Why, and what should you have done?
questions.a: A change of nav source can drop the autopilot to a lower mode such as wings level [[30:52|RMH 7-3]]. Anticipate it, select heading mode first, then act and verify on the mode annunciators [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]. Stepping down to a lower level of automation is often the right move [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

questions.q: How do you handle the passenger and the workload?
questions.a: Fly first. Ask the passenger to hold questions, ask ATC for a vector or delay if rushed [[30:47|RMH 6-4]], and stop, look and read before pressing buttons [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]]. ATC is part of your team, and an emergency gets priority if needed [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

questions.q: What should you have planned before takeoff?
questions.a: Know the risk area from NOTAMs, plan extra fuel, and plan to use conventional NAVAIDs and approaches at the destination [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]]. Pick airports with non-GPS approaches, such as VOR MON airports [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]].

skills.do: Tune and identify the VOR (or load the GPS waypoint from a current database), check flags and integrity, and verify accuracy as your equipment requires.
skills.practice: On the ramp, do a VOT or ground checkpoint check and log date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]. In the GPS, check the database expiration date before every IFR flight [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

skills.do: Say your position relative to the station or waypoint: radial and distance, or bearing and distance.
skills.practice: At random times, center the CDI with FROM and call out your radial; add DME or GPS distance for a fix [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

skills.do: Set the course to be intercepted and say which side of it you are on.
skills.practice: Before each intercept, set the course you will fly so there is no reverse sensing, and picture yourself on an HSI-style view [[23:257|IFH 9-14]] [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].

skills.do: Intercept the course inbound or outbound at a suitable angle, leading the turn so you do not overshoot.
skills.practice: Work the IFH steps (difference, double it, 20° to 90°) on paper, then in flight [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. Practice arc intercepts with a 0.5 NM lead [[23:260|IFH 9-17]].

skills.do: Hold airspeed ±10 knots, altitude ±100 ft, and selected headings ±5° (ACS IR.V.A.S5).
skills.practice: Trim for level flight before setting radios, and scan attitude and altitude between every nav task.

skills.do: Keep the CDI within ¾ scale, and if flying a DME arc, stay within ±1 NM of it (ACS IR.V.A.S6).
skills.practice: Bracket wind corrections: 20°, then half [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. On arcs, correct 10° to 20° for each ½ mile off [[23:261|IFH 9-18]].

skills.do: Recognize a VOR, DME or GPS failure (flags, lost ident, integrity alerts, position jumps) and report it to ATC.
skills.practice: Have your instructor fail a receiver or the GPS, then make a full 91.187 report out loud [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]. Learn the jamming signs [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]].

skills.do: Use the MFD or moving map to watch position, wind drift and the big picture.
skills.practice: Compare TRK with DTK and your heading on every leg [[23:255|IFH 9-12]] [[1:396|PHAK 16-9]]. Set map scale and orientation for the phase of flight [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]].

skills.do: If the examiner asks, use the autopilot to make course intercepts.
skills.practice: Practice heading mode to an intercept heading, arm nav, and verify armed and engaged annunciators; first under VFR with an instructor [[30:52|RMH 7-3]].

skills.do: Use single-pilot resource management: plan, prioritize, use ATC and automation wisely.
skills.practice: Brief each intercept before you start it and ask ATC for time if rushed [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Choose the automation level for the workload [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

quiz.q: With normal sensitivity, a full-scale VOR CDI deflection means you are about how far off course?
options: 20° or more
12° or more
quiz.why: Full deflection means 12° or more off course. 2° is only the edge of the center circle [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].

quiz.q: The TO flag is showing on your VOR. What does that tell you?
options: The selected course would take you to the station
The airplane's heading is pointed directly at the station
You are flying inbound on the radial set in the OBS
You have passed the station and are now flying away from it
quiz.why: TO/FROM shows where the selected course takes you, not where you are heading [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].

quiz.q: On a standard VOR CDI, the OBS is set to the reciprocal of the course you are flying. The needle is right of center. To get back on course you:
options: Turn right, toward the needle
Hold heading; the needle will center
Turn left, away from the needle
Re-center the needle with the OBS
quiz.why: That is reverse sensing, so you turn away from the needle. Set the OBS to your intended course to avoid it [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

quiz.q: You are on the 070° radial and want to intercept the 100° radial. What intercept angle does the IFH method give?
quiz.why: Difference 30°, doubled = 60°, which is within the 20° to 90° limits [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

quiz.q: What is the most error allowed using a designated airborne VOR checkpoint?
quiz.why: Airborne checkpoint: ±6°. ±4° is for a test signal or surface checkpoint [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)]].

quiz.q: Inbound on a radial at 130 knots to join the 10 DME arc. Where do you start the turn?
options: 10.5 DME
11 DME
10 DME
9.5 DME
quiz.why: A 0.5 NM lead is enough at 150 knots or less. 9.5 DME is the lead when outbound [[23:260|IFH 9-17]] [[23:261|IFH 9-18]].

quiz.q: No wind, on a DME arc with the bearing pointer on the wingtip, you are about 1 NM outside the arc. What does the IFH suggest?
options: Turn 20° away from the station
Turn 90° toward the station
Turn 20° toward the station
Hold heading; the arc will come to you
quiz.why: ½ to 1 mile outside with the pointer on the wingtip: turn 20° toward the facility [[23:261|IFH 9-18]].

quiz.q: How many satellites does RAIM need to detect a bad satellite?
options: 5, or 4 plus baro-aiding
4, or 3 plus baro-aiding
6, or 5 plus baro-aiding
3 plus WAAS
quiz.why: Detection needs 5 or 4 with baro-aiding. 6 (or 5 with baro) is for FDE, which also excludes the bad satellite [[33:89|AIM 1-1-17]].

quiz.q: Within 30 NM of the airport with the approach armed, what is the GPS full-scale CDI sensitivity?
options: ±5 NM
±1 NM
±2 NM
quiz.why: Arming changes en route ±5 NM to terminal ±1 NM within 30 NM [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17]].

quiz.q: Your autopilot shows NAV in white and HDG in green. What is the autopilot doing?
options: Flying the heading bug, with NAV armed, not engaged
Tracking the nav course, with heading mode only armed
Flying wings level in roll mode, with neither mode engaged
Both modes are failed, so the autopilot has disconnected
quiz.why: Green annunciators are engaged; white ones are armed but not engaged [[30:52|RMH 7-3]].

quiz.q: Which VOT frequency is listed for Groton?
quiz.why: The table lists Groton at 110.25 [[29:90|IPH Figure 2-50]].

quiz.q: A checkpoint sign reads VOR 116.4, 147 degrees 4.1 NM. Which frequency do you tune?
quiz.why: The first line of the sign gives the VOR frequency [[29:90|IPH Figure 2-51]].

quiz.q: At that sign, the VOR should show which radial?
quiz.why: The sign is the DME and VOR check radial, 147 degrees [[29:90|IPH Figure 2-51]].

quiz.q: In the DME example, the first segment is 5 NM and the second is 10 NM. What is in the encircled DME arrow?
quiz.why: The encircled arrow gives the total mileage, 15 NM [[2:82|Chart Users' Guide p 82]].

quiz.q: On a VHF airway, an arrow beside a fix points:
options: Toward the next fix on the airway
Away from the VHF/UHF NAVAID that forms the fix
Toward magnetic north
Toward the nearest airport
quiz.why: Off-set arrows show the facility forming a fix. For VHF/UHF the arrow points away from the NAVAID [[2:82|Chart Users' Guide p 82]].

takeaways: Tune, identify, check flags. No ident means don't use it.
FROM + centered needle = the radial you are on. Set the course you will fly to avoid reverse sensing.
Intercept: difference, double it, 20° to 90°, lead the turn. Track: 20° correction, then half.
VOR check every 30 days: ±4° ground, ±6° airborne, 4° dual. Log it.
DME arc: 0.5 NM lead at 150 knots or less; correct 10° to 20° per ½ mile; stay within ±1 NM.
GPS: RAIM or WAAS integrity, current database, CDI ±5, ±1, ±0.3 NM. GPS may fly a DME arc using the arc's DME facility.
Anticipate, act, verify the automation. Report nav failures to ATC under 91.187.
cfi_notes: IFH 9-14 writes the intercept heading as "205° + 090° = 295°." That shortcut only works because the angle is 90°. Teach it as the desired course turned toward the course side by the intercept angle, and have the student sketch the picture.

IFH 9-16 and 9-17 say VOT and checkpoint locations are in the A/FD and mention an endorsement for the 30-day check. Current AIM 1-1-4 says the Chart Supplement, and 14 CFR 91.171(d) requires date, place, bearing error and a signature [[33:71|AIM 1-1-4]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].
IFH 9-26 names only TSO-C129 for IFR GPS and gives older WAAS station counts. Teach the current AIM list: TSO-C129(), C196(), C145(), C146() [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17]].
Examiners often probe reverse sensing, the legality of flying a DME arc by GPS, and what the student does at ¾-scale deflection. Make students say the GPS arc rule from IFH 9-27 out loud.
Students chase the needle near the station. Have them fly a fixed heading and bracket, and remind them the needle gets more sensitive as they close in [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].
Fly arcs three ways: with a bearing pointer, with a CDI only, and with GPS distance. The CDI-only method (re-center at 2° to 4°) is the one students least expect [[23:261|IFH 9-18]].
For autopilot intercepts, have the student call out each annunciator change. Then fail the GPS source and watch the mode reversion [[30:52|RMH 7-3]].

IFH 9-27 and 9-28 give the older "GPS substitution for ADF or DME" steps. Current AIM 1-2-3 lets a suitable RNAV system (TSO-C129/-C145/-C146 approved for IFR en route and terminal) fly a DME arc, hold, and fix positions even when the NAVAID is out of service, but not fly a LOC course without raw data or replace the final approach NAVAID; it points to AC 90-108 for details [[33:116|AIM 1-2-3]] [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]] [[33:118|AIM 1-2-3]]. Teach the IFH steps as technique and the AIM as the rule.
gaps: Button-by-button GPS navigator and autopilot procedures (OBS or leg mode, CDI scale display, nav mode arming) come from the POH/AFM supplement for the installed equipment; the sources give general rules only.
AC 90-108 (RNAV on conventional procedures) and AC 90-100A are not in the uploaded sources; GPS substitution is taught from AIM 1-2-3 and IFH 9-27.
No source gives a numeric lead for joining an arc above 150 knots (only "proportionately greater") or specific correction angles for GPS-based arcs.
No source converts the ¾-scale ACS limit into degrees (VOR) or miles (GPS); the lesson gives only the full-scale values.
RMI and ADF operation are mentioned only as they apply to DME arcs; NDB tracking is outside this lesson's focus.

activities.title: Read the VOR
activities.intro: Tap an indication, then what it means.

pairs.r: The index shows the radial you are on
The selected course takes you to the station
Reverse sensing: turn away from the needle

pairs.l: NAV or OFF flag in view

activities.title: Name the parts of the HSI
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.
activities.why: These are the HSI parts named in Figure 9-13. The course deviation bar shows left or right of the course set with the course arrow [[23:255|IFH 9-12]] [[23:118|IFH 5-23]].

activities.title: Intercept a radial
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Center the CDI with FROM to find the radial you are on
Find the difference to the radial you want and double it (20° to 90°)
Set the OBS to the desired radial or inbound course
Turn to the intercept heading and hold it
Lead the turn as the CDI starts to center
Turn to the course heading and bracket the wind

activities.title: Whose limitation is it?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Zone of confusion over the station
Propeller rpm can make the needle swing ±6°
Reads your height above the station when overhead
Groundspeed good only flying straight to or from the station
Needs 5 satellites, or 4 plus baro, for RAIM
Antenna can be shadowed in a bank

activities.title: Work the numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: You are on the 040° radial and want to intercept the 075° radial. Using the IFH method, what intercept angle do you use?
items.why: Difference 075 - 040 = 35°. Double it: 70°, which is between 20° and 90° [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

items.q: You are on the 300° radial and want to track the 330° radial inbound (course 150°). The course is to your left, and the IFH method gives a 60° intercept angle. What heading do you fly?
items.why: Difference 30°, doubled = 60° [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. Turn 60° left of the 150° course: 150 - 60 = 090°.

items.q: Inbound on a radial at 125 knots groundspeed to join the 14 DME arc. At what DME reading do you start the turn?
items.why: A 0.5 NM lead is enough at 150 knots or less, so 14 + 0.5 = 14.5 DME [[23:260|IFH 9-17]].

items.q: You fly 5,000 ft above the elevation of a VOR/DME. Beyond what distance from the station is slant range error negligible?
items.why: 1 NM or more for each 1,000 ft above the facility: 5 × 1 = 5 NM [[23:262|IFH 9-19]].

items.q: Outbound on a radial at 140 knots groundspeed to join the 12 DME arc. At what DME reading do you start the turn?
items.why: A 0.5 NM lead is enough at 150 knots or less [[23:260|IFH 9-17]]. Outbound, subtract it: 12 - 0.5 = 11.5 DME [[23:261|IFH 9-18]].

activities.title: Around the arc, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are flying N123AB, a single-engine airplane with a VOR/LOC receiver, DME, an IFR GPS and an autopilot. Today you will join the 10 DME arc of a VORTAC in the clouds.

steps.s: Before departure you see the last VOR check was 33 days ago. Your airport has a VOT.
options: Depart on the GPS and skip the VOR check, since the GPS will cover you
Check that both VOR needles move and the flags clear, then depart
Depart now and do an airborne check later, once you are in the clouds
Do a VOT check within ±4° and log date, place, error and signature
steps.why: The check must be within 30 days to use VORs under IFR. A VOT check allows ±4°, and you must log date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171]] [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

steps.s: Airborne, you tune the VORTAC. The needle looks good but you hear no ident at all.
options: Use it; the needle is centered and steady
Do not rely on it; tell ATC and use another source
Turn the volume to zero and rely on the needle
Use it only for distance, not course
steps.why: Removing the ident warns that the facility may be off the air for maintenance and unreliable [[33:87|AIM 1-1-11]]. The ident is the only positive identification [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3]].

steps.s: The ident returns and ATC confirms the VORTAC is fine. You track inbound on a radial at 140 knots to join the 10 DME arc.
options: Start the turn at 11.5 DME
Start the turn at 10.0 DME
Start the turn at 10.5 DME
Start the turn at 9.5 DME
steps.why: At 150 knots or less, a 0.5 NM lead is enough: 10.5 DME. 9.5 DME is the lead when you are outbound [[23:260|IFH 9-17]] [[23:261|IFH 9-18]].

steps.s: On the arc, the bearing pointer is on the wingtip and the DME reads 10.8 and rising. The wind is pushing you away from the station.
options: Turn about 20° away from the station and keep the pointer behind the wingtip
Hold heading and wait for the wind to carry you back to the arc
Turn about 20° toward the station, pointer ahead of the wingtip
Turn 90° toward the station and hold it until the DME reads 10.0
steps.why: ½ to 1 mile outside with the pointer on the wingtip: turn 20° toward the facility. With wind pushing you away, keep the pointer ahead of the wingtip [[23:261|IFH 9-18]]. Stay within ±1 NM (ACS IR.V.A.S6).

steps.s: Later, coupled to GPS on the arc, the map position jumps two miles and a position-error message appears.
options: Keep the autopilot coupled to GPS and wait for the position to recover
Climb 1,000 ft without a clearance to get better satellite reception
Reset the GPS while the autopilot keeps flying the last heading
Use heading mode, fly the arc on raw VOR/DME data, and tell ATC
steps.why: A large position shift and position-error warnings can mean jamming or spoofing. Verify with conventional NAVAIDs, be ready to revert, and tell ATC promptly [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]] [[33:120|AIM 1-2-4]]. Step down the automation level to keep control [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

steps.s: Then the VOR flag drops into view and stays. You still have DME but no course guidance.
options: Report it with aircraft ID, equipment, degree of impairment and help wanted
Keep flying the arc by DME alone, and say nothing to ATC until you are on the ground
Squawk 7600 and continue as if you had lost two-way radio communications
Switch the GPS back on and continue the approach without telling ATC about the VOR
steps.why: Under IFR in controlled airspace, report nav malfunctions to ATC as soon as practical with those four items [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]. A flag means the signal is not usable [[23:254|IFH 9-11]].

activities.title: True or false: automation and failures
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Changing the nav source can make the autopilot drop to a lower mode, such as wings level.
cards.why: Yes. A pilot who does not expect this can end up confused and overloaded [[30:52|RMH 7-3]].

cards.s: If the autopilot does something unexpected, keep it engaged and reprogram until it works.
cards.why: No. Reduce the level of automation, fly by hand and take time to fix it [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

cards.s: Under IFR in controlled airspace you must report a nav receiver failure to ATC as soon as practical.
cards.why: Yes, with aircraft ID, equipment affected, degree of impairment and help wanted [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]].

cards.s: RAIM fully protects you from GPS spoofing.
cards.why: No. RAIM is only partly effective against spoofing-type disruption, and ATC may be the only one to notice [[33:87|AIM 1-1-13]].

cards.s: A hand-held GPS may be used as your IFR navigation source if it has a current database.
cards.why: No. VFR and hand-held GPS units are not authorized for IFR navigation [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

cards.s: Checking GPS position against VOR or DME can help you spot a bad GPS signal.
cards.why: Yes. Routine crosschecks against VOR or DME can reveal a compromised GPS signal [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]].

activities.title: VOR check limits and symbols
activities.intro: Tap a term, then the answer that matches it.

pairs.l: Error limit on a VOT or ground checkpoint
Error limit on an airborne checkpoint
Dual VOR check, most difference allowed

final_quiz.q: You are on the 340° radial and want to track the 010° radial inbound (course 190°). The IFH method gives a 60° intercept. What heading do you fly?
final_quiz.why: Double the 30° difference = 60° [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. Flying 190° inbound, the course is to your left, so turn 60° left of 190°: 130°. 070° comes from adding the angle to the radial, which only works for a 90° intercept.

final_quiz.q: At a VOT, you center the CDI and the OBS reads 177° with TO showing. What is the result?
options: Out of limits: a VOT must read 0° FROM exactly
Within limits: 3° error, under the ±4° allowed
Within limits only if checked again in the air
Out of limits: the TO flag should show FROM at 180°
final_quiz.why: A VOT should give 180° TO (or 0° FROM) [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]], and the limit is ±4° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]].

final_quiz.q: You cruise 6,000 ft above a VORTAC's elevation. Inside about what distance is DME slant range error no longer negligible?
options: 1 NM
3 NM
6 NM
12 NM
final_quiz.why: Slant range error is negligible at 1 NM or more for each 1,000 ft above the facility: 6 NM here [[23:262|IFH 9-19]].

final_quiz.q: Your VOR check was 35 days ago and the VOR is not on an approved maintenance procedure. Can you use VOR navigation under IFR today?
options: Yes; a VOR check stays good for 90 days from the date it was done
Yes, as long as the station's ident is heard and the needle is steady
Yes, if a second VOR on the same station agrees within 6°
No; do a new check within limits and log it first
final_quiz.why: The check must be within the preceding 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]], logged with date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]]. Dual VORs must agree within 4°, not 6°.

final_quiz.q: Two independent VORs tuned to the same station show bearings of 212° and 217°. Can this count as your 91.171 check?
options: Yes, it is within 6°
Yes, dual checks have no limit
No, dual checks are only allowed in the air
No, the most allowed between them is 4°
final_quiz.why: A 5° spread is over the 4° maximum for a dual-system check [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]].

final_quiz.q: You will fly the 15 DME arc of a VORTAC using GPS in place of DME. Which waypoint do you make active?
options: The airport reference point
The VORTAC the arc is based on
The initial approach fix at the start of the arc
Any named fix along the arc
final_quiz.why: Only the DME facility the arc is based on is acceptable; fly the arc by GPS distance from it [[23:270|IFH 9-27]].

final_quiz.q: You are 40 NM from the destination with a GPS approach loaded and armed. What full-scale CDI sensitivity should you see?
options: ±5 NM
±1 NM
±2 NM
final_quiz.why: With the approach armed, the CDI stays at en route ±5 NM until you are within 30 NM of the airport, then changes to ±1 NM. ±0.3 NM comes only at the FAWP [[33:96|AIM 1-1-17]].

final_quiz.q: Your IFR GPS is TSO-C129 (no WAAS). Which equipment must also be installed and working for an en route IFR flight?
options: Nothing else, because RAIM monitoring covers any outage of the ground-based NAVAIDs
A second hand-held GPS receiver as a backup for the panel-mounted unit, and nothing more
Avionics for the ground-based NAVAIDs on the route and any required alternate
An ADF receiver only, since the GPS replaces the VOR and DME
final_quiz.why: With TSO-C129() or C196() receivers, the avionics for all ground-based facilities on the route to the destination and alternate must be installed and operational [[33:94|AIM 1-1-17]].

final_quiz.q: Near a NOTAMed area, your GPS position jumps and the clock shows the wrong time. What is the best action?
options: Keep the autopilot coupled to GPS, since RAIM will flag any bad position data
Crosscheck with VOR/DME, revert to conventional navigation, tell ATC
Reset the GPS receiver and continue on the magenta line once it recovers
Climb to get better satellite reception and keep going on the GPS course
final_quiz.why: Position jumps and clock errors are signs of jamming or spoofing. Verify with conventional NAVAIDs, be ready to revert, and notify ATC promptly [[33:119|AIM 1-2-4]] [[33:120|AIM 1-2-4]]. Inside a known NOTAMed test area, you need to report it to ATC only if you need help [[33:120|AIM 1-2-4]].

final_quiz.q: Which item is NOT required in a 91.187 malfunction report?
options: How much your IFR capability is impaired
The equipment affected
The date of your last VOR check
The help you want from ATC
final_quiz.why: The report needs aircraft ID, equipment affected, degree of impairment and assistance desired [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187(b)]].

final_quiz.q: Approaching a VOR on unfamiliar routes, the needle swings briefly. How do you confirm positive station passage?
options: The needle swings full scale once
The DME stops changing
The OFF flag appears
The TO/FROM indicator reverses
final_quiz.why: Some stations show brief needle swings like station passage, so use the TO/FROM indicator to confirm positive station passage [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]] [[23:259|IFH 9-16]].

final_quiz.q: Tracking a 360° course inbound, the needle drifts left. You turn to 340° and the needle centers. What is your next heading?
options: 360°, the course
350°, half the correction
330°, more correction
340° and change the OBS to center the needle
final_quiz.why: After the 20° correction centers the needle, decrease it by half and make smaller corrections [[23:257|IFH 9-14]]. Changing the OBS turns tracking into homing.

final_quiz.q: You are hand-flying an intercept while ATC gives you a new clearance and you must load a new approach. What does the RMH suggest?
options: Turn the autopilot off so you can feel the airplane and stay in the loop
Load the approach first, then fix the heading once the box is done
Ignore the clearance until you are established on the intercept
Let the autopilot fly the intercept while you do the other tasks
final_quiz.why: The autopilot can make the control inputs while you complete other tasks, reducing workload [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

final_quiz.q: Which VOT frequency is listed for Hartford?
final_quiz.why: The table lists Hartford at 108.20 [[29:90|IPH Figure 2-50]].

final_quiz.q: The checkpoint sign reads 147 degrees 4.1 NM. What DME reading do you expect at the sign?
options: 4.1 NM
147 NM
final_quiz.why: The sign gives the distance as 4.1 NM [[29:90|IPH Figure 2-51]].

final_quiz.q: Your last VOR check was 45 days ago. Can you fly IFR using the VOR system today without a new check?
options: Yes, if the VOR looks accurate
Yes, if you are on an airway
No, the check must be within 30 days
Yes, for 60 days
final_quiz.why: Unless the equipment is kept on an approved procedure, the VOR must have been checked within the preceding 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: You check two independent VORs against each other on the same station. They read 3 degrees apart. Is that within limits?
options: Yes, the limit is 4 degrees
No, the limit is 1 degree
No, the limit is 2 degrees
Yes, any difference is fine
final_quiz.why: With dual VORs, the maximum permissible variation between the two bearings is 4 degrees [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(c)]].

final_quiz.q: On the airport, a ground checkpoint shows your VOR is off by 5 degrees. Is it legal for IFR?
options: Yes, up to 6 degrees is allowed
No, the limit is plus or minus 4 degrees
Yes, up to 10 degrees is allowed
Only at night
final_quiz.why: At a VOT or airport checkpoint the maximum error is plus or minus 4 degrees. The 6 degree limit is for airborne checks [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(2)]].
